puzzle_statement: Galilea, Farazi & Mare (2026) find, across 101 economies at the FIRM level, that electronic-payment use eases credit constraints and that the effect is larger where credit-information depth is lower (payment records substituting for a missing credit file). Does the same coverage-moderated pattern hold at the INDIVIDUAL level -- i.e. is the within-economy digital-payment / formal-borrowing association larger in economies with thinner 2019 credit-bureau/registry coverage -- in the 2024 Global Findex? Candidate explanations if not: E1 digital-footprint substitution; E2 a coverage floor / non-linearity; E3 an account-access channel (digital payments mark formal-system inclusion, not an incremental signal); E4 supply-side heterogeneity (lenders in thin-coverage economies cannot act on payment data).

foundational.predicts: Asymmetric information causes credit rationing; anything that improves lender information about borrower type can expand credit at the margin. This is the default the substitution hypothesis builds on.

Information sharing through credit bureaus/registries reduces adverse selection and increases aggregate lending; the value of a new information source is higher where existing information sharing is weaker.

foundational.cite: Berger & Udell (2006), Journal of Banking & Finance 30(11):2945-2966
foundational.predicts: Lenders choose among distinct lending technologies (financial-statement, relationship, credit-scoring, transaction) according to the information environment; whether a digital-payment trace is usable depends on which technology the lender operates.

foundational.cite: Demirguc-Kunt, Klapper, Singer & Ansar (2022), The Global Findex Database 2021 (World Bank, ISBN 9781464818974); updated by Klapper, Singer, Starita & Norris (2025), The Global Findex Database 2025: Connectivity and Financial Inclusion in the Digital Economy (World Bank, ISBN 9781464822049; ~148,000 adults, 141 economies, 2024 wave)
foundational.predicts: Findex measurement framework; adults who receive digital payments into an account use other formal financial services (saving, borrowing) more than average. Descriptive by construction.

recent.cite: Galilea, Farazi & Mare (2026), Policy Research Working Paper 11287, World Bank
recent.contribution: Across 101 economies, payment digitalization alleviates FIRM credit constraints, especially for small firms and in economies with weaker credit infrastructure, lower financial development and larger informal sectors -- the parent result Study 5 checks at the individual level.
recent.method: World Bank Enterprise Surveys pooled cross-section; firm and country characteristics; heterogeneity by credit-information depth. Descriptive/associational.

recent.cite: Alok, Ghosh, Kulkarni & Puri (2024), NBER Working Paper 33259
recent.contribution: India's UPI cross-platform payment system increased financial deepening and brought NEW borrowers into formal credit; banks expanded to prime borrowers, only fintechs served new-to-credit; credit growth strongest where bank-account penetration was recent and internet affordable; no rise in defaults.
recent.method: Staggered UPI adoption across India; credit-bureau microdata; difference-in-differences style. Identified, single country.

recent.cite: Ghosh, Vallee & Zeng (2025), NBER Working Paper 34148
recent.contribution: In FinTech lending, greater use of cashless payments predicts better loan terms and lower default rates for small firms -- payment data has real information content for credit.

recent.cite: Cornelli, Frost, Gambacorta, Rau, Wardrop & Ziegler (2023), Journal of Banking & Finance (BIS Working Paper 887, 2020)
recent.contribution: Cross-country drivers of fintech/bigtech credit volumes; such credit is larger where GDP per capita is higher, banking is less competitive/regulated, ease of doing business is greater, and where there are fewer bank branches. Concludes alternative credit COMPLEMENTS rather than substitutes for bank credit.
recent.method: Cross-country panel of fintech/bigtech credit volumes (new database).

recent.cite: Bazarbash & Beaton (2020), IMF Working Paper WP/20/150
recent.contribution: 109 countries, 2015-2017: marketplace consumer lending grows where financial DEPTH declines, especially in low-income countries -- market-level evidence for digital credit 'filling the gap' left by traditional lenders.
recent.method: Cross-country regressions of fintech credit volumes on financial-development measures.

recent.cite: Agarwal, Alok, Ghosh & Gupta (2019/rev.), ISB working paper
recent.contribution: Alternative data from a borrower's mobile phone (apps, call logs, 'deep social footprints') substitute for the credit-bureau score in default prediction and, in counterfactual ML analysis, would expand credit to the credit-invisible without raising default.
recent.method: Proprietary single FinTech-lender data, India; machine-learning prediction + counterfactual.

closest_papers.question: Do electronic payments ease firm credit constraints, and more so where credit information is thin?
closest_papers.identification: Cross-sectional, firm + country controls, heterogeneity splits; associational (no causal claim)
closest_papers.finding: Yes for firms; effect larger where credit-information depth is lower, financial development lower, informality higher
closest_papers.distance_from_puzzle: unit: firms/SMEs vs individual adults; outcome: self-reported credit-constraint status vs realised formal borrowing (Findex fin22a); moderator: depth-of-credit-information index vs max(2019 bureau, registry) coverage; data: Enterprise Surveys vs Global Findex. Same hypothesis and moderation logic, different population and data -- Study 5 is the individual-level external-population check.

closest_papers.question: Did India's UPI (cross-platform digital payments + consent-based data sharing) expand access to formal consumer credit?
closest_papers.data: Indian credit-bureau microdata + UPI adoption; ~300m individuals
closest_papers.finding: Digital payments brought new-to-credit borrowers into formal credit via fintechs; strongest where bank accounts were recently opened and internet affordable
closest_papers.distance_from_puzzle: population: India only vs 97 economies; method: natural experiment vs cross-section; outcome: bureau-observed new originations vs Findex self-reported borrowing; NO cross-country credit-information-coverage moderation. The sub-national 'strongest where accounts are recent' gradient is directionally TOWARD H-000500 (bigger where the formal system is newer/thinner), which Study 5 does not find across countries -- a live tension to discuss.

closest_papers.cite: Berg, Burg, Gombovic & Puri (2020), Review of Financial Studies 33(7):2845-2897
closest_papers.question: How much information about consumer default is in a digital footprint, relative to a credit-bureau score?
closest_papers.data: ~250,000 purchases at one German e-commerce lender
closest_papers.finding: Simple digital-footprint variables match or exceed the bureau score; crucially, the footprint COMPLEMENTS rather than substitutes for bureau information, and improves access + lowers default
closest_papers.distance_from_puzzle: population: one lender, one high-income country vs 97-economy adult population; outcome: default prediction vs borrowing incidence; does not test a country-coverage moderation. Its 'complement not substitute' result is a central competing explanation for Study 5's reversal (E3).

closest_papers.cite: Agarwal, Alok, Ghosh & Gupta (2019), ISB WP
closest_papers.question: Can mobile-phone digital footprints substitute for bureau scores and expand inclusion?
closest_papers.finding: Yes -- alternative data substitutes for the bureau score and would extend credit to the credit-invisible
closest_papers.distance_from_puzzle: single lender, India; a scoring/counterfactual exercise, not observed population borrowing; no cross-country moderation; deep phone data, not the Findex made/received-a-payment binary.

closest_papers.question: Does cashless-payment use improve FinTech loan terms and performance for small firms?
closest_papers.finding: More cashless-payment use -> better loan terms, lower default for small firms
closest_papers.distance_from_puzzle: unit: small firms; outcome: loan pricing / default, not borrowing incidence; platform data not Findex; no country-coverage moderation.

closest_papers.cite: Cornelli, Frost, Gambacorta, Rau, Wardrop & Ziegler (2023), JBF / BIS WP 887
closest_papers.question: What drives cross-country differences in fintech & bigtech credit volumes?
closest_papers.finding: Larger where GDP p.c. higher, banking less competitive, fewer bank branches, better ease of doing business; alternative credit complements rather than substitutes
closest_papers.distance_from_puzzle: unit: aggregate provider volumes vs individual borrowing; outcome: supply of digital credit vs use of formal-institution credit; no individual moderation. Complementarity finding relevant to E3.

closest_papers.question: Can fintech credit fill the credit gap left by traditional lenders?
closest_papers.finding: Marketplace consumer lending grows where financial depth declines, esp. low-income countries -- market-level substitution/gap-filling
closest_papers.distance_from_puzzle: unit: aggregate volumes vs individuals; period 2015-17 vs 2024; outcome: fintech credit supply vs formal-institution borrowing; substitution result at MARKET level contrasts with Cornelli et al. -- literature is split.

explanation_map.explanation: E1 -- digital-payment/footprint substitution: the payment-borrowing slope is steeper where 2019 credit-information coverage is thinner (H-000500's prediction)
ruled_out_by: not ruled out in the literature; NOT reproduced at the individual level in Study 5 -- interaction is significantly negative

explanation_map.explanation: E2 -- coverage floor / non-linearity: in the ~24 economies with <10% coverage there is no cross-sectional room for a payment record to substitute at the margin
supported_by: consistent with Berger & Udell (2006) lending-technology logic; no direct cross-country test found
tested_against: Study 5 drop-zero-coverage and drop-lowest-quartile checks -- interaction stays negative, so a pure floor is not the whole story
ruled_out_by: partially, by Study 5's own sensitivity checks

explanation_map.explanation: E3 -- account-access channel: digital-payment activity in thin-coverage economies mainly marks formal-system inclusion, not an incremental lender-legible signal
supported_by: Berg et al. (2020) (footprint complements, not substitutes)
Alok et al. (2024) (credit growth concentrated where bank accounts are recent -> account access is the binding margin)
tested_against: Study 5 account-holders-only restriction -- interaction shrinks toward zero and loses precision, consistent with a composition story but imprecise; conditioning on account ownership is itself an endogenous collider
ruled_out_by: not ruled out; currently the most consistent with both the outside evidence and Study 5's sensitivities

explanation_map.explanation: E4 -- supply-side heterogeneity: lenders in thin-coverage economies lack the systems/technology to act on a digital-payment history
supported_by: Alok et al. (2024) (only fintechs, not banks, served new-to-credit)
tested_against: not testable with Global Findex (demand-side survey only)

methods_catalog.strategy: Cross-country descriptive regression with country fixed effects + heterogeneity splits
methods_catalog.known_weakness: No within-country identification of the moderator; the cross-level interaction can be driven by compositional differences in who uses digital payments across countries; no exogenous variation.
Single country; rollout timing may be endogenous to local conditions; external validity to other institutional settings unclear.

methods_catalog.strategy: Single proprietary lender data + predictive / ML counterfactual
methods_catalog.known_weakness: Selection into the lender; speaks to information content and one lender's originations, not to population-level access; cannot identify aggregate credit-market effects.
Supply-side, provider-reported; no borrower characteristics; measurement of 'fintech credit' inconsistent across countries; endogeneity of financial-development regressors.

unresolved_questions: Substitute vs complement: micro evidence (Berg et al. 2020) and one market study (Cornelli et al. 2023) find payment/footprint data COMPLEMENTS bureau information; Galilea et al. (firms) and Bazarbash & Beaton (market, low income) find substitution / gap-filling. The margin may be level-dependent (firm vs individual) and channel-dependent (account access vs incremental signal). Unsettled.
Whether the firm-level coverage-moderation result (Galilea et al. 2026) extends to individual retail borrowers across countries -- not tested in the individual-level literature located here.

Whether cross-country Doing Business 'Getting Credit' coverage is a usable moderator: the series was discontinued by the World Bank on 16 Sept 2021 after the WilmerHale investigation found data irregularities in DB 2016-2020, and the Getting Credit indicator specifically was among those manipulated for China (DB2018) and Saudi Arabia (DB2020) -- both economies are in the Study 5 sample.

Reverse causality at the interaction level: a disbursed formal loan generates account activity and digital payments; whether that feedback differs by country coverage (e.g. more cash-based lending where coverage is thin) is untested and could itself produce a coverage gradient.

candidate_gaps.gap: Whether the firm-level digital-payment x credit-information interaction of Galilea, Farazi & Mare (2026) holds for INDIVIDUAL retail borrowers is untested in a cross-country individual-level design. The Global Findex has been used extensively for individual determinants of formal borrowing (demographics, income, education, account ownership) but not, in the literature located here, for a digital-payment x 2019-credit-information-coverage interaction on formal borrowing.
left_open_by: Alok, Ghosh, Kulkarni & Puri (2024) (India only, no cross-country coverage moderation)
Berg et al. (2020) (one lender, one country)
Demirguc-Kunt et al. (2022) / Klapper et al. (2025) (descriptive, no moderation test)

candidate_gaps.gap: The substitute-vs-complement question for payment data and formal borrowing at the INDIVIDUAL level across heterogeneous credit-information environments is unsettled and has not been adjudicated with a demand-side population survey.

current_claims: S1: 'Whether the same pattern holds for individuals is not established.'
S1: the Global Findex 'has been used mainly to describe digital-payment adoption and broad financial-inclusion outcomes rather than to test this specific moderation.'
S2: 'We claim only an individual-level descriptive analogue and external-population check of the Galilea et al. pattern. We make no ... novelty claim.'
manuscript_language_check.verdict: SUPPORTABLE AS NOVELTY_CANDIDATE at PARTIAL adequacy. No individual-level cross-country Findex test of this specific interaction was located. Recommended phrasing: 'we are not aware of an individual-level cross-country test of this interaction' / 'the literature appears to provide limited evidence on ...' -- not 'first' or 'no prior study' (already contract-banned). The claim that Findex is used 'mainly to describe' is fair but should cite the determinants literature (individual logistic regressions of formal borrowing) so it is not read as 'nobody has run a regression'.
must_also_fix: Reference list: 'Galilea, G. W.' -> 'Galilea, M.' (Manuel Galilea); cite as Policy Research Working Paper 11287, World Bank.

S1 para 1: a 2024-wave fact ('a majority of adults ... make or receive a digital payment') is cited to Demirguc-Kunt et al. (2022); cite Klapper, Singer, Starita & Norris (2025) instead. The 2025 report figure is 62% of adults in low- and middle-income economies (82% of account owners) in 2024.
Berg et al. (2020): the manuscript implies it supports the substitution mechanism; it explicitly finds the digital footprint COMPLEMENTS the bureau score. Reframe -- this strengthens Study 5's E3.

Add Cornelli et al. (2023) and Alok, Ghosh, Kulkarni & Puri (2024) to Related Literature; the latter is the closest individual-level paper and its sub-national gradient runs opposite to Study 5's cross-country result.

Bazarbash & Beaton (2020): correct the description -- 109 countries, 2015-2017, fintech credit volumes vs financial development; finding is market-level substitution ('filling the gap'), strongest in low-income countries.

search_adequacy_justification: Twelve query families across WebSearch plus World Bank, NBER, SSRN, IMF, BIS and RePEc repositories; 58 hits screened, 3 full texts + 11 abstracts/summaries reviewed. The closest-paper neighbourhood is well populated (firm-level cross-country, individual single-country natural experiment, single-lender micro, market-level cross-country), which makes a direct scoop of the exact individual-level cross-country Findex coverage-moderation test unlikely. It cannot be excluded that a World Bank Policy Research Working Paper companion to Galilea et al. (2026), or a Global Findex research working paper, runs a similar individual-level cut; a systematic EconLit/Scopus/Google Scholar pass and a check of the Galilea et al. paper's own robustness sections would be needed to move to ADEQUATE.
